The partition key determines how items are distributed across physical partitions: items that share a partition key value form a logical partition so related data stays co‑located, making queries within that logical partition efficient and scoping transactions to a single logical partition [1]. A good partition key (high cardinality) also helps spread storage and request volume evenly [2].

Use Azure Service Bus as the messaging layer and run your worker in Azure Container Apps with a KEDA Service Bus queue depth scale rule.

- Azure Service Bus is the managed message broker with queues and competing consumers, suited for work-distribution scenarios (order processing, pipelines) and supports retries/TTL/dead-lettering for poison messages [3][1][5].  
- Container Apps uses KEDA-based autoscaling and the canonical pattern for queue-driven workers is a KEDA scale rule on Service Bus queue depth (worker scales out as the queue deepens and back to zero when it drains) [2][8].  
- Container Apps can scale to zero replicas and incurs no compute charges while at zero, so the worker costs nothing when idle [8].

The reliability pillar recommends deploying redundant instances across fault domains so no single failure takes the workload down [2]. Availability zones are those fault domains within a region — physically separate data centers with independent power, cooling, and networking — and a zone‑reduant deployment spreads replicas across zones so the loss of a single zone does not take the application down [2][1]. Designing for failure (expecting components will fault) aligns with using zones for redundancy to make faults survivable [3][2].
